messages.subject: Multilevel IRT/Ideal Point Models: Additive Redundant Parameterization Problem
parts:
Hi,

I am trying to implement the rescaling method discussed in Gelman and Hill (2007) and  Bafumi(2005) http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/171.pdf, but I keep getting this error message

" Error in function stan::prob::bernoulli_logit_log(N4stan5agrad3varE): Logit transformed probability parameter[0]  is 1.#QNAN:0, but must not be nan!Rejecting proposed initial value with zero density.
Initialization failed after 100 attempts.  Try specifying initial values, reducing ranges of constrained values, or reparameterizing the model.
error occurred during calling the sampler; sampling not done "

Here is the model


data {
  int<lower=1> J;                // number of students
  int<lower=1> K;                // number of questions
  int<lower=1> N;                // number of observations
  int<lower=1,upper=J> jj[N];    // student for observation n
  int<lower=1,upper=K> kk[N];    // question for observation n
  int<lower=0,upper=1> y[N];     // correctness of observation n
}
parameters {
  vector[J] a_raw;
  vector[K] b_raw;
  vector<lower=0>[K] g_raw;
  real<lower=0> mu_g_raw;
  real mu_b_raw;
  real mu_a_raw;
  real<lower=0> sigma_a_raw;
  real<lower=0> sigma_b_raw;
  real<lower=0> sigma_g_raw;
} 
transformed parameters {
  vector[J] a;
  vector[K] b;
  vector[K] g;
  vector[N] p;
  real scale;
  real shift;

  shift <- mean(a);
  scale <- sd(a);

  a <- (a_raw - shift)/scale;
  b <- (b_raw - shift)/scale;
  g <- g_raw*scale;


  for (n in 1:N)
  p[n]<-g[kk[n]]*(a[jj[n]] - b[kk[n]]) ;
  

}
model {

  mu_a_raw ~ normal(0, 10);
  sigma_a_raw ~ cauchy(0,3);
  a_raw ~ normal(mu_a_raw, sigma_a_raw);
  
  mu_b_raw ~ normal(0, 10);
  sigma_b_raw ~ cauchy(0,3);
  b_raw ~ normal(mu_b_raw, sigma_b_raw);

  mu_g_raw ~ uniform(0, 10);
  sigma_g_raw ~ cauchy(0,3);
  g_raw ~ lognormal(mu_g_raw, sigma_g_raw);
  
  y ~ bernoulli_logit(p);

}

Thanks
Rick,

shift <- mean(a);
  scale <- sd(a);

  a <- (a_raw - shift)/scale;
  b <- (b_raw - shift)/scale;
The first two lines should come after the last two. Both shift and scale will be NaN at the time of evaluation in the original model.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] typo in ARM model
parts:
OK, I see what's going on. This is NOT a good way to code
these models. This model relies on Andrew's trick for BUGS of
specifying an ill-defined posterior to sample from, then
attempting to pull it all back into something with reasonable
n_eff and Rhat through standardization. Here's the offending
code in our example:

> transformed parameters {
> vector[J] a;
> vector[K] b;
> vector[K] g;
> vector[N] p;
> real scale;
> real shift;
>
> shift <- mean(a);
> scale <- sd(a);

> a <- (a_raw - shift) / scale;
> b <- (b_raw - shift) / scale;
> g <- g_raw * scale;
>
> for (n in 1:N)
> p[n]<-g[kk[n]]*(a[jj[n]] - b[kk[n]]);

The problem here is that the raw values are not identified.

The problem is that the posterior for the parameters is improper.
And what you see is that Stan's HMC is effcient enough to race all over
the posterior and at least realize it's undefined.

There's a chapter on problematic posteriors that goes through
an example of the effects of such non-identified models. (Look at the
plot of the long ridge, which is what happens for this kind of example.)

This model needs to be recoded so that it's properly identified.

We're working on rewriting all the ARM models, which are a pretty direct translation
of what's in Gelman and Hill, and thus not guaranteed to work.

This looks like a good place to start!

For models that don't have data we can release, we can simulate
data according to the model. I want to bring up the question of how
to simulate predictors for regressions --- it seems like for proper testing
we shouldn't make them all independent.

- Bob

It's a reparameterization. You have an
additive non-identifiability, which you can fix
by fixing one of the coefficients. And you have
a multiplicative non-identifiability that can get
fixed by fixing one of the scales, say the student
abilities, to normal(0,1). And then there's a sign
non-identifiability, which you can fix by constraining
the discrimination (g) to b positive. (Unless it's
an item-response model, then I'm not sure what to do
about the sign --- Andrew and Jennifer discuss in their
book.)

- Bob

> OK, I see what's going on. This is NOT a good way to code
> these models. This model relies on Andrew's trick for BUGS of
> specifying an ill-defined posterior to sample from, then
> attempting to pull it all back into something with reasonable
> n_eff and Rhat through standardization. Here's the offending

>
> > transformed parameters {
> > vector[J] a;
> > vector[K] b;
> > vector[K] g;
> > vector[N] p;
> > real scale;
> > real shift;
> >

> > scale <- sd(a);

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] typo in ARM model
parts: If I am not mistaken, for a d-dimensional model, if we specify a normal(0,1) prior on  each on the ability parameters (factors), we would still need d*(d-1)/2 additional constraints on the discrimination parameters. So for a two dimensional model, we would need to impose one restriction on the discrimination(loading) matrix. But these restrictions won't take care of reflective invariance and label switching. In Bayesian Factor Analysis, the positive lower triangular identification scheme is usually used to to mitigate rotational invariance, sign flips, and label switching. Has anyone fit a model in stan using the positive lower triangular identification scheme?

We don't have a solution for label switching, I'm afraid.
There's a discussion in the manual, but all the possible solutions
we've come up with or seen from others are flawed.

I don't know about the rotational indeterminancy.  Is there
a mathematical constraint on the params that solve it?

indeterminacy problem.  

- Bob

parts:
Hi Bob,

For a factor model y=Lf +e, where f~ N(0,Sigma) , I think there are three important cases to consider:

1. The positive lower triangular (PLT) identification scheme mentioned here http://apps.olin.wustl.edu/faculty/zhou/GZ-RFS96.pdf , where Sigma=I (identity matrix) and the the diagonal entries of L are polarity constrained.
2.The modified PLT where the factors,f, are still orthogonal but the elements of diagonal of Sigma Aguilar, O. & West, M.(2000) Bayesian dynamic factor models and portfolio allocation.
3.. Sigma is a correlation matrix, but now instead of requiring D(D-1)/2 constraints on L, we need D(D-1) to ensure local uniqueness under rotation and the polarity constraint to ensure global rotational uniqueness.This paper lists the conditions http://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11336-012-9259-3

But as this paper shows https://www.stat.washington.edu/research/reports/2011/tr589.pdf , imposing constraints is problematic.

I'll try work on something and if I get a working Stan model, I'll send it to you.

Rick,
